podcast.body: The inaugural smash hit for PIR, this song was not interpreted as a failed romantic relationship, but rather as a commentary on the systemic treatment of Black men and women in America, a theme Greil Marcus characterized as "music of worry and confinement." "Backstabbers is not really about a relationship gone bad. It's about how black men and women were treated in America."

srcs.episode: Ep. 37 - Philly Soul and the Sound of the 70s

podcast.body: This song marked a significant milestone for The O'Jays, becoming their first number one R&B single in 1972. It is characteristic of the "Philadelphia sound" produced by Kenny Gamble and Leon Huff, evident in its prominent use of strings. Before this breakout hit, The O'Jays had a long history performing on the "Chitlin circuit" in the South. Scholars like Alice Eccles suggest that while the song can be interpreted as relationship betrayal, it also carries a deeper political commentary, possibly echoing Dr. King's sentiments about white moderates and reflecting a broader theme of betrayal within the Black Power movement. "Backstabbers was the first number one R&B single for the OJs who had been playing what was called the Chitlin circuit of the South for a long time before that song took off in 1972."
